title: Corrosion Behavior of Cold-Sprayed 316L Coatings: Effects of Deposition Temperature and Surface Condition
abstract: Abstract The passivation behavior of cold-sprayed 316L stainless steel coatings deposited onto SAE 1020 carbon steel was investigated with particular emphasis on the influence of surface condition and deposition temperature. Coatings produced at gas temperatures of 650-825 °C exhibited thicknesses of ~ 450-520  µ m and porosity levels of ~ 5-7 vol.%, with microstructures characterized by interparticle boundaries and incomplete bonding typical of cold-sprayed deposits. Electrochemical performance was evaluated in 0.6 M NaCl solution using open circuit potential (OCP), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and cyclic potentiodynamic polarization (CPP). In the polished condition, the coatings consistently exhibited a shift toward more noble OCP values compared to both the as-sprayed state and the SAE 1020 substrate, indicating enhanced surface stability. Despite moderate polarization resistance and the presence of microstructural heterogeneities, EIS results revealed capacitive responses associated with passive-like surface films. Cyclic polarization further demonstrated that polished coatings are capable of sustaining anodic polarization without abrupt current increase, in contrast to the active behavior of the substrate, and in some cases showed evidence of repassivation. These findings indicate that surface finishing plays a critical role in stabilizing passive-like behavior, even in the presence of residual porosity. Overall, the results demonstrate that polished cold-sprayed 316L coatings effectively promote passivation and significantly improve the corrosion resistance of carbon steel substrates in chloride-containing environments.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Cold spray is a solid-state coating technology in which micron-sized particles (< 50  µ m) are accelerated to high velocities (~ 700-1000 m s −1 ) and deposited onto a substrate to form a coating (Ref  1 ,  2 - 3 ). In contrast to conventional thermal spray processes (Ref  4 ), particle melting does not occur prior to impact, as the typical deposition temperatures are below 1000 °C; instead, bonding is achieved through intense plastic deformation induced by the particle’s kinetic energy upon high-velocity impact (Ref  5 ,  6 ,  7 - 8 ). Owing to its solid-state nature, cold spray avoids disadvantages associated with high-temperature processing, such as excessive oxidation, undesirable phase transformations, and grain coarsening, while often preserving refined microstructures. These features make the process attractive for coating, repair, and additive manufacturing applications in sectors such as oil and gas, aerospace, and chemical processing, where both structural integrity and corrosion resistance are required (Ref  2 ,  3 ,  9 ).

The deposition of a more corrosion-resistant material onto a less noble substrate by cold spray has attracted increasing attention in recent years since it allows the deposition of protective metallic layers without melting, thereby minimizing thermal degradation and preserving the chemistry of corrosion-resistant alloys (Ref  3 ,  10 ). However, the corrosion performance of cold-sprayed coatings depends not only of the intrinsic corrosion resistance of the feedstock material, but also of the microstructural features inherent to the process, such as surface roughness, porosity, interparticle boundaries, and incomplete bonding may create preferential pathways for electrolyte penetration and lead to electrochemical responses that differ significantly from those of the corresponding bulk alloy (Ref  11 ,  12 - 13 ).

AISI 316L is particularly attractive for cold spray because of its good corrosion resistance, oxidation stability, and capacity for plastic deformation (Ref  14 ,  15 ). However, despite these advantages, cold-sprayed 316L coatings do not generally reproduce the behavior of bulk 316L in the as-sprayed condition. Previous studies have shown that such deposits commonly exhibit heterogeneous microstructures containing interparticle boundaries, incompletely bonded interfaces, residual porosity, and locally deformed skin-core particle structures (Ref  8 ,  16 ,  17 ). In addition, coating quality is strongly affected by spray parameters, particularly gas temperature, gas pressure, particle size distribution, and standoff distance, all of which influence particle deformation and densification (Ref  18 ,  19 - 20 ).

Because of these intrinsic heterogeneities, several studies have focused on post-treatments to improve the properties of cold-sprayed 316L. Heat treatment, vacuum annealing, hot isostatic pressing, and laser remelting have all been reported to reduce porosity, enhance interparticle bonding, promote recrystallization, and improve mechanical performance (Ref  16 ,  19 ,  21 ,  22 ,  23 - 24 ). Improved corrosion resistance after heat treatment or laser post-treatment has been associated with reduced porosity and healing of weak interparticle interfaces (Ref  22 ,  25 ,  26 ). These studies indicate that corrosion performance in cold-sprayed 316L is closely linked to microstructural features such as porosity, particle-particle bonding, and the accessibility of electrolyte through interfacial defects.

Surface condition is another critical factor influencing the corrosion behavior of thermally sprayed coatings (Ref  27 ,  28 - 29 ). In general, as-sprayed surfaces are characterized by high roughness, partially bonded particles, oxide inclusions, and exposed intersplat or interparticle boundaries, which can act as preferential sites for localized corrosion and facilitate electrolyte penetration into the coating (Ref  29 ,  30 ). Surface finishing processes, such as grinding and polishing, are commonly applied to reduce surface roughness, remove loosely bonded particles, and produce a more homogeneous surface (Ref  27 ,  28 ). In conventional thermal spray coatings, such treatments have been widely reported to improve corrosion resistance by limiting defect accessibility and promoting the formation of more stable passive films (Ref  29 ,  31 ).

However, in cold-sprayed coatings, the effect of surface finishing is less straightforward. While polishing may reduce surface irregularities, it can also expose subsurface defects, interconnected porosity, and previously occluded interparticle boundaries, potentially increasing the electrochemically active area and altering the corrosion response. Therefore, the role of surface condition in cold-sprayed stainless steel coatings remains an open question, particularly regarding whether surface finishing leads to a true improvement in corrosion resistance or simply modifies the electrochemical interface without mitigating intrinsic microstructural heterogeneities.

Deposition temperature is also one of the most critical processing parameters in cold spray, as it directly influences particle velocity, plastic deformation, and interparticle bonding during impact. Higher gas temperatures generally promote increased particle velocities and enhanced plastic deformation, leading to improved coating densification, reduced porosity, and stronger interparticle cohesion (Ref  18 ,  19 - 20 ). As a result, deposition temperature is expected to affect not only the microstructural integrity of the coating but also its corrosion performance, particularly by modifying the connectivity of defects and the accessibility of electrolyte pathways. Although several studies have reported improvements in mechanical properties and, in some cases, corrosion resistance with increasing deposition temperature or subsequent densification treatments, the isolated effect of deposition temperature on the electrochemical behavior of cold-sprayed 316L coatings remains insufficiently understood. In particular, it is still unclear whether variations in deposition temperature alone, without post-processing, are sufficient to significantly alter corrosion mechanisms, or whether surface-related factors may play a more dominant role. Therefore, a systematic evaluation of deposition temperature, in conjunction with surface condition, is required to elucidate its true contribution to the corrosion behavior of cold-sprayed coatings.

Despite the growing body of work on post-processing strategies to enhance coating performance, the combined influence of deposition temperature and surface condition on the corrosion behavior of cold-sprayed 316L coatings remains insufficiently understood. Deposition temperature plays a fundamental role in defining the coating microstructure by controlling particle velocity, deformation, and interparticle bonding, thereby influencing porosity and defect connectivity. At the same time, surface finishing governs the characteristics of the electrochemical interface, affecting surface roughness, defect exposure, and electrolyte accessibility. In practical applications, coatings are often used under varying combinations of these conditions, where both bulk microstructural features and surface state may jointly control corrosion processes.

Thus, an assessment of these two parameters is essential to clarify their individual and combined effects. In this context, the present work investigates the corrosion behavior of cold-sprayed 316L stainless steel coatings deposited onto SAE 1020 carbon steel, explicitly considering surface condition and the deposition temperatures as the central variables through a comparison between as-sprayed and polished states. The study combines microstructural characterization with open circuit potential (OCP), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and cyclic potentiodynamic polarization (CPP) to elucidate how surface condition interacts with intrinsic coating heterogeneity to control the overall electrochemical response.

sections.heading: Cold Spray Processing
paragraphs: The coatings were produced by cold spray deposition of a commercial AISI 316L stainless steel powder (Sandvik Osprey 5-38  μ m) onto SAE 1020 carbon steel substrates. The deposition was carried out by Polycontrols Technologies Inc. (Canada), using and (Plasma Giken’s PCS-100). During processing, nitrogen (N 2 ) was used as the propellant gas at a constant pressure of 940 psi, while the gas temperature was varied to evaluate its influence on coating formation and microstructural development. Three deposition temperatures were investigated: 650, 800, and 825 °C. The resulting coatings were designated as C1, C2, and C3, corresponding to deposition temperatures of 650, 800, and 825 °C, respectively.

sections.heading: Microstructural Characterization
paragraphs: The specimens were sectioned, mounted in Bakelite, and prepared following standard metallographic procedures. Grinding was performed using SiC papers with grit sizes of 240, 320, 400, 600, 800, 1200, and 2000, followed by polishing with an alumina suspension. After preparation, the specimens were cleaned with acetone and dried.

Porosity was quantified by image analysis using ImageJ software from binarized optical micrographs acquired at 50× magnification using a ZEISS Axio optical microscope. Approximately 10-15 randomly selected images were analyzed for each specimen, covering representative coating regions. The porosity fraction was calculated as the ratio between pore area and total analyzed area. Mean porosity values and standard deviations were determined from the analyzed images.

Further microstructural characterization was performed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) using an Inspect-FEI and Quanta FEI 400 microscopes. Observations were conducted in both secondary electron (SE) and backscattered electron (BSE) modes to assess particle deformation, coating morphology, and pore distribution. Confocal microscopy (CM) LEXT 3D Measuring LASER microscopy OLS4100 Olympus was used for roughness measurements in as-sprayed and polished conditions.

sections.heading: Electrochemical Characterization
paragraphs: All electrochemical measurements were performed in triplicate to ensure reproducibility, using a three-electrode cell configuration connected to a Gamry 600 + potentiostat. A saturated calomel electrode (SCE) and a platinum sheet were used as the reference and counter electrodes, respectively. The cold-sprayed coatings, the SAE 1020 substrate, and a hot-rolled AISI 316L stainless steel sample were used as working electrodes. Prior to testing, all specimens were degreased with acetone and dried. Electrochemical measurements were conducted on the top surface of the coatings, corresponding to the plane perpendicular to the build direction. The coatings were tested in the as-sprayed and in polished conditions.

Cyclic potentiodynamic polarization (CPP) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were performed in a 0.6 M NaCl solution prepared using high-purity NaCl (> 99%) and demineralized water. The exposed working electrode area was 0.3 cm 2 . Before polarization measurements, the working electrode was stabilized at open circuit potential (OCP) for 1 h to ensure steady-state conditions. Potentiodynamic polarization tests were conducted from − 250 mV relative to the OCP up to a current density of 10 −3  A cm −2 , using a scan rate of 1 mV s −1 . The corrosion current density ( i corr ) was estimated by extrapolation of the cathodic branch, which exhibited Tafel-like behavior.

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy measurements were carried out over a frequency range from 10 5  Hz to 10 −2  Hz (10 points per decade), using an AC perturbation amplitude of 10 mV rms  around the OCP. The impedance data were analysed using the Measurement Model approach proposed by Watson and Orazem (Ref  32 ,  33 ), in which the experimental spectra are fitted using a series of Voigt elements. This method enables the determination of electrochemical parameters such as solution resistance, polarization resistance, and effective capacitance without relying on subjective equivalent circuit selection.

sections.heading: Microstructural Features
paragraphs: Figures  1 (a-f) present optical micrographs of the cross-sections of the cold-sprayed coatings deposited at different gas temperatures, highlighting coating thickness and porosity distribution. Continuous coatings were obtained on the SAE 1020 substrate under all processing conditions, with thicknesses ranging from approximately ~450 to ~500  µ m (Table  1 ). No macroscopic defects, such as cracks or delamination at the coating–substrate interface, were observed, indicating the structural integrity of the deposits. Fig. 1 Optical micrographs of the cold-sprayed 316L stainless steel coatings deposited on SAE 1020 carbon steel at different gas temperatures: (a, b) 650 °C (C1), (c, d) 800 °C (C2), and (e, f) 825 °C (C3). (a), (c), (e) show cross-sections revealing the interface between coating and substrate, and (b), (d), (f) present longitudinal-section of the cold-sprayed coatings Table 1 Thickness and porosity of the cold-sprayed coatings (C1, C2, and C3) determined by image analysis of cross-sectional and longitudinal micrographs Coatings Thicknesses,  µ m Porosity-cross-sections, vol.% Porosity-longitudinal–sections, vol.% C1 522 ± 11 7.54 ± 0.96 6.08 ± 0.97 C2 455 ± 26 6.63 ± 0.48 5.13 ± 1.07 C3 457 ± 27 5.72 ± 0.47 5.12 ± 1.03

The micrographs reveal a homogeneous distribution of porosity throughout the coatings, which is a characteristic feature of cold-sprayed stainless steel deposits. This porosity originates from incomplete bonding between plastically deformed particles during high-velocity impact, leading to the formation of interparticle boundaries and residual voids (Ref  2 ,  3 ). Quantitative image analysis (Table  1 ) indicates porosity levels ranging from ~ 5.1 ± 1.1 to ~ 7.5 ± 0.9 vol.%, consistent with values typically reported for cold-sprayed alloys (Ref  18 ,  19 ,  21 ,  34 ,  35 ).

A slight but consistent reduction in porosity is observed with increasing gas temperature. Quantitative image analysis revealed a progressive reduction in porosity with increasing gas temperature, decreasing from 7.54 ± 0.96 vol.% for C1 (650 °C) to 5.72 ± 0.47 vol.% for C3 (825 °C). This trend can be attributed to the increase in particle velocity and the associated enhancement in plastic deformation at higher gas temperatures, which promote improved interparticle bonding and reduce the formation of voids within the coating (Ref  3 ).

Top-view SEM micrographs acquired in backscattered electron (BSE) mode (Fig.  2 ) illustrate the surface morphology of the coatings in both as-sprayed and polished conditions. The as-sprayed surfaces (Figs.  2 a-c) exhibit pronounced roughness, characterized by partially deformed particles and surface asperities inherent to the deposition process. In contrast, the polished surfaces (Figs.  2 d-f) display a significantly smoother and more uniform morphology, enabling clearer observation of the underlying microstructural features. Fig. 2 SEM micrographs acquired in backscattered electron (BSE) mode showing the top surface of cold-sprayed 316L stainless steel coatings deposited on SAE 1020 carbon steel at different gas temperatures: (a) 650 °C [C1], (b) 800 °C [C2], and (c) 825 °C [C3] in the as-sprayed condition; and (d) 650 °C [C1], (e) 800 °C [C2], and (f) 825 °C [C3] after polishing

Figure  3 (a-f) show higher-magnification SEM images of the coatings deposited at different gas temperatures. The microstructure is typical of cold spray deposits, consisting of plastically deformed particles that undergo partial flattening upon high-velocity impact with the substrate and previously deposited layers. This results in a globular-to-lamellar architecture with residual porosity primarily located at interparticle interfaces, a well-established intrinsic feature of cold spray coatings (Ref  2 ,  3 ). Fig. 3 SEM micrographs of the cold-sprayed 316L stainless steel coatings deposited on SAE 1020 carbon steel at different gas temperatures: (a, b) 650 °C (C1), (c, d) 800 °C (C2), and (e, f) 825 °C (C3). Figs. 3(a), (c), (e) show the overall microstructure of the coatings, while (b), (d), (f) present higher-magnification images highlighting inter-particle bonding, porosity, plastically deformed particles, localized defects, and fragmented interfacial features characteristic of cold-sprayed coatings

Although a slight decrease in porosity is observed with increasing gas temperature, differences in particle deformation and densification are not readily distinguishable from SEM observations alone. All coatings exhibit a heterogeneous microstructure, including interparticle gaps and irregularly shaped pores, as well as some larger and potentially interconnected voids. These features are particularly relevant, as they may act as preferential pathways for electrolyte ingress and localized corrosion, and as stress concentrators that can influence mechanical performance [2, 3. 10, 11]. These heterogeneities are commonly observed in cold-sprayed coatings due to the solid-state deposition mechanism and incomplete local interparticle deformation and bonding.

Surface roughness measurements obtained by confocal microscopy (Fig.  4 ) further highlight the influence of post-processing. The as-sprayed coatings exhibit relatively high surface roughness, with values in the range of approximately 5-8  µ m, consistent with the presence of undeformed and semi-deformed particles. After polishing, a substantial reduction in roughness is observed, reaching values below 0.1  µ m (approximately 0.046-0.075  µ m), corresponding to a decrease of nearly two orders of magnitude. This smoothing effect is critical for subsequent characterization and performance evaluation, particularly in corrosion and tribological applications. Fig. 4 Three-dimensional surface topography obtained by confocal microscopy for the cold-sprayed coatings in the as-sprayed and polished conditions at different gas temperatures: 650 °C (C1), 800 °C (C2), and 825 °C (C3)

From a functional perspective, the observed microstructural architecture is advantageous for protective applications. Despite the presence of porosity and interparticle boundaries, the coatings form a continuous and adherent barrier on the substrate surface, effectively isolating it from the external environment. Furthermore, the use of a corrosion-resistant alloy such as 316L enables the coating to maintain passive behavior, thereby mitigating the electrochemical activity of the underlying carbon steel. In this context, the primary role of the coating is not to replicate the properties of fully dense bulk 316L stainless steel, but rather to provide an effective protective layer that significantly enhances the corrosion resistance of the SAE 1020 substrate.

sections.heading: Open Circuit Potential (OCP)
paragraphs: Figure  5  presents the evolution of the open circuit potential (OCP) for the investigated materials during 60 min of immersion in 0.6 M NaCl solution. At the end of the exposure period, the SAE 1020 substrate and hot-rolled AISI 316L exhibited OCP values of − 0.724 and − 0.185 V SCE , respectively, representing the expected behavior of an active carbon steel and a highly passive stainless steel. Fig. 5 Evolution of the open circuit potential (OCP) with immersion time for the SAE 1020 substrate, hot-rolled AISI 316L, and C1, C2, and C3 cold-sprayed coatings in the as-sprayed and polished conditions. Measurements were carried out for 60 min in 0.6 M NaCl solution at room temperature and open air

The cold-sprayed coatings exhibited intermediate OCP values between those of the substrate and the bulk 316L. In the as-sprayed condition, OCP values of − 0.268 ± 0.098 V SCE  (C1), − 0.443 ± 0.002  V SCE  (C2), and − 0.462 ± 0.019 V SCE  (C3) were obtained. After polishing, a consistent shift toward more positive potentials was observed, with values of − 0.201 ± 0.023 V SCE , − 0.367 ± 0.090 V SCE , and − 0.393 ± 0.066 V SCE  for C1, C2, and C3, respectively.

Importantly, despite their inherent porosity and microstructural heterogeneity, all cold-sprayed coatings exhibited significantly more noble potentials than the SAE 1020 substrate. This indicates that the coatings effectively modify the electrochemical response of the system, acting as a protective barrier that reduces the thermodynamic tendency for corrosion of the underlying steel. In this sense, the coatings fulfil their primary function as corrosion-resistant layers, even in the as-sprayed condition. The observed shift toward more positive OCP values after polishing further highlights the influence of surface condition on the electrochemical response. This behavior can be attributed to the removal of surface irregularities and loosely bonded particles, leading to a more stable and uniform surface that favor passive film formation (Ref  10 ,  36 ).

sections.heading: Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS)
paragraphs: Figures  6  and  7  present the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) results in the form of Nyquist and Bode plots for the cold-sprayed coatings in both as-sprayed and polished conditions. The experimental impedance data,  Z(ω) exp , were analyzed using the measurement model (MM) approach based on a Voigt-type representation,  Z(ω) MM , enabling a robust and physically consistent description of the electrochemical response. The corresponding fitted parameters are summarized in Table  2 . Fig. 6 Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) results and fitting using the measurement model (MM) for the substrate, hot-rolled 316L, and C1, C2, and C3 cold-sprayed coatings in the as-sprayed condition. (a) Model employed for fitting; (b) Nyquist diagrams; (c) detailed view of the high-frequency region of the Nyquist diagrams present in Fig. 6b; (d) Bode magnitude (|Z|) plots; and (e) Bode phase angle plots. Measurements were performed in 0.6 M NaCl solution at room temperature and open air Fig. 7 Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) results and fitting using the measurement model (MM) for the substrate, hot-rolled 316L, and C1, C2, and C3 cold-sprayed coatings in the polished condition. (a) Model employed for fitting; (b) Nyquist diagrams; (c) detailed view of the high-frequency region of the Nyquist diagrams present in Fig. 7b; (d) Bode magnitude (|Z|) plots; and (e) Bode phase angle plots. Measurements were performed in 0.6 M NaCl solution at room temperature and open air Table 2 Parameters from measurement model (MM) approach Alloy Condition R Ω , Ω cm 2 R p , kΩ cm 2 C eff ,  µ F cm −2 χ 2  (×10 −3 ) Voigt elements C1 As-sprayed 32 ± 2 3.0 ± 0.8 1.8 ± 0.2 31 ± 7 7 Polished 31 ± 4 2.5 ± 1.5 4.3 ± 3.3 78 ± 10 7 C2 As-sprayed 32 ± 2 1.5 ± 0.9 7.0 ± 1.7 18 ± 9 7 Polished 31 ± 2 3.3 ± 1.5 11.6 ± 1.6 23 ± 2 7 C3 As-sprayed 27 ± 1 3.2 ± 0.9 11.3 ± 1.2 19 ± 15 7 Polished 29 ± 1 2.8 ± 0.7 17.4 ± 1.9 9 ± 2 7 AISI 316L Hot-rolled Polished 36 512 6.4 5 7 SAE 1020 Substrate Polished 28 ± 1 7.6 ± 1.9 17.8 ± 3.4 6 ± 2 7

The electrochemical parameters, including effective capacitance ( C eff ), polarization resistance ( R p ), and ohmic resistance ( R Ω ), were determined by fitting the experimental impedance spectra using the measurement model (MM) regression approach (Ref  32 ,  33 ), as presented in Figs.  6  and  7  and summarized in Table  2 . This approach involves adjusting a physically based impedance representation,  Z(ω) MM ,  to experimental data,  Z(ω) exp .
The simulated data obtained using the measurement model (MM) approach showed good agreement with the experimental EIS results, with low fitting errors (see Table  2 ).

From Figs.  6 (e),  7 (e) and Table  2 , the ohmic resistance ( R Ω ) values at high frequencies (10 5 -10 4  Hz) are approximately 30 Ω cm 2  for all samples, reflecting the electrolyte resistance governed by the high concentration of mobile ions (Na +  and Cl − ) in solution. In this frequency range, the phase angle approaches 0°, as expected for predominantly resistive behavior.

At low frequencies (10 −2  Hz, Figs.  6 d and  7 d), significant differences in impedance magnitude are observed among the materials. The hot-rolled AISI 316L exhibits the highest impedance (|Z| 10 mHz  ~ 2.7 × 10 5  Ω cm 2 ), followed by the SAE 1020 substrate (|Z| 10 mHz  ~ 6.3 × 10 3  Ω cm 2 ), while the cold-sprayed coatings present lower but still measurable |Z| 10 mHz  values ranging from ~ 1.3 × 10 3  to ~ 2.2 × 10 3  Ω cm 2 .

The Bode phase angle plots (Fig.  6 e,  7 e) show that the hot-rolled alloy maintains a phase angle close to − 80° over a broad frequency range (10 −1 -10 1  Hz), which is characteristic of a stable and protective passive film on stainless steels (Ref  37 ,  38 ). In contrast, the substrate and cold-sprayed coatings exhibit less negative phase angles and a narrower capacitive region, indicating a more heterogeneous electrochemical interface. Although the more noble OCP values of the coatings compared with the SAE 1020 substrate suggest the development of passive-like behavior, the impedance response indicates that the electrochemical behavior is also strongly influenced by microstructural heterogeneities inherent to the cold spray process, such as porosity, interparticle boundaries, localized defects, and surface roughness (Ref  11 ,  25 ).

The Nyquist plots (Figs.  6 b,c and  7 b,c) further support these observations, with the hot-rolled AISI 316L showing the largest semicircle diameter, corresponding to the highest polarization resistance ( R p ). While the cold-sprayed coatings exhibit lower  R p  values, their response remains significantly resistive, indicating that they act as effective barriers that modify the electrochemical behavior of the system. Importantly, the coatings limit the direct exposure of the substrate to the electrolyte, thereby contributing to an overall improvement in corrosion resistance. The Nyquist diagrams (Figs.  6 b,c,  7 b,c) show that the hot-rolled AISI 316L presents a larger semi-circle diameter compared to the substrate and cold-sprayed coatings. In Table  2  and Figs.  6 (d),  7 (a), (d) consistent tendency can be seen in which the hot rolled sample exhibits the highest polarization resistance ( R p ), confirming its superior corrosion resistance compared to both the substrate and the cold-sprayed coatings.

Compared to the coatings in both as-sprayed and polished conditions, the SAE 1020 substrate shows an intermediate corrosion behavior, while the cold-sprayed coatings present lower  R p  values, which can be attributed to their heterogeneous microstructure, including porosity, inter-particle boundaries, and defects inherent to the cold spray process (Ref  10 ,  11 ,  12 - 13 ). It is important to mention that such microstructural heterogeneity may also contribute to a higher variability in electrochemical measurements, particularly in EIS, which is highly sensitive to local interfacial properties. This may explain the relatively large uncertainties observed in Table  2  and the difficulty in establishing clear tendencies for  R p  values. Although the open circuit potential results indicated a shift toward more noble values after polishing (Fig.  3 ), the effect of this surface treatment on  R p  was not consistently observed for all coatings.

In addition, the severe plastic deformation associated with particle impact during cold spraying may introduce a high density of crystalline defects, residual strain, and stored deformation energy, which can further influence the electrochemical activity and passive film stability of the coatings. Recent studies have suggested that deformation-induced microstructural features may significantly affect corrosion behavior in cold-sprayed materials by modifying passive film formation and localized electrochemical response (Ref  39 ). This behavior suggests that the electrochemical response of the coatings results from a combination of passive-like film formation and deformation/microstructure-related effects inherent to the cold spray process.

Furthermore, although relatively high uncertainties are observed for some  C eff  values (see Table  2 ), an apparent increase in effective capacitance is observed after polishing for all coatings. The variation in  C eff  suggests a modification of the electrochemical interface, which may be associated with changes in the electrochemically active surface area, surface roughness at different length scales, or alterations in the passive film characteristics. The lower capacitance values observed for the hot-rolled AISI 316L are consistent with the presence of a compact and stable passive film, whereas the higher capacitance values of the substrate and cold-sprayed coatings reflect a more complex and heterogeneous interface. The increase in capacitance after polishing further supports the notion of enhanced accessibility of the electrochemical interface (Ref  10 ).

Again, it is important to emphasize that the EIS tests were performed at rest, i.e., around the open circuit condition. Note that both carbon steel and the cold sprayed samples present a similar  R p  values. However, these results (Figs.  6  and  7 ) did not provide the persistence of the polarization resistance as the system is polarized. It means that, even starting if a similar  R p  value, the cold spray may be more effective to restrain active corrosion upon polarization thanks to the ability to form a passive like film, which will be discussed in the following section, focusing on the cyclic polarization curves. Indeed, note that the coatings C1 (as sprayed and polished) and C2 (a-sprayed) in Table  2  present  C eff  values more close to the AISI 316L Hot-rolled stainless steel than the substrate. This values of  C eff  in the order of few  µ F cm −2  is typically ascribed to passive film, an indication that the  C eff   suggests a passive-like layer which can restrain the increase of corrosion upon polarization.

It is important to emphasize that the EIS measurements were performed under rest conditions, i.e., around the open circuit potential. Under these conditions, both the SAE 1020 substrate and the cold-sprayed coatings exhibit comparable  R p  values. However, this apparent similarity does not reflect the full protective capability of the coatings under more aggressive conditions. EIS at OCP does not capture the ability of the material to sustain passivity or resist corrosion upon anodic polarization. In this context, cold-sprayed coatings present a clear advantage.

Despite exhibiting moderate  R p  values, several coatings, particularly C1 (as-sprayed and polished) and C2 (as-sprayed), show  C eff  values closer to those of the hot-rolled AISI 316L than to the carbon steel substrate, Table  2 . Capacitance values in the order of a few  µ F cm −2  are typically associated with the presence of passive films, suggesting that these coatings can form passive-like surface layers even in the as-deposited condition. This behavior is highly relevant from a corrosion protection standpoint. While the coatings do not reach the polarization resistance of fully dense bulk 316L, their ability to develop passive-like films enables them to restrain the increase in corrosion activity under polarization.

Therefore, the protective performance of cold-sprayed coatings should not be assessed solely based on  R p  values at open circuit, but rather on their capacity to modify the corrosion mechanisms of the system and to delay the onset of active dissolution. Overall, these results reinforce the effectiveness of cold-sprayed 316L coatings as protective layers. Even in the presence of porosity and microstructural heterogeneity, the coatings combine barrier effects with passive-like behavior, providing a robust and practical strategy for enhancing the corrosion resistance of carbon steel substrates.

sections.heading: Cyclic Potentiodynamic Polarization (CPP)
paragraphs: To further elucidate the corrosion behavior of the investigated materials, cyclic potentiodynamic polarization (CPP) tests were performed to evaluate their anodic response and ability to sustain passivity under increasing applied potentials. This technique provides insight into the stability of the passive film, as well as the susceptibility to localized corrosion and the capacity for repassivation after breakdown.

Figure  8  presents the CPP curves obtained in 0.6 M NaCl solution for the substrate, hot-rolled AISI 316L, and the cold-sprayed coatings in both as-sprayed and polished conditions. The corrosion potential ( E corr ), corrosion current density ( i corr ), transpassivation potential ( E transp ), are detailed in Table  3 . This analysis is particularly relevant for assessing the protective performance of cold-sprayed coatings, as it enables the evaluation of their behavior beyond open circuit conditions, providing insight into their ability to limit corrosion propagation and maintain passive-like behavior under anodic polarization. Fig. 8 Potentiodynamic polarization curves obtained for the SAE 1020 substrate, hot-rolled AISI 316L, and C1, C2, and C3 cold-sprayed coatings in 0.6 M NaCl solution: (a) as-sprayed condition and (b)  polished condition. As expected, the hot-rolled AISI 316L exhibits the most noble corrosion potential ( E corr ), the lowest corrosion current density ( i corr ), and a well-defined passive region, confirming its superior corrosion resistance. In contrast, the SAE 1020 substrate displays the most negative  E corr  and a rapid increase in current density with increasing potential, characteristic of active dissolution and the absence of a stable passive film.

The cold-sprayed coatings, in both as-sprayed and polished conditions, exhibit intermediate behavior between the hot-rolled 316L and the substrate, similar results under different environmental conditions were reported in (Ref  25 ). In general, the coatings show less negative  E corr  values compared to the substrate, indicating a more noble electrochemical response. Additionally, the polarization curves suggest the development of passive-like regions, allowing the potential to increase without a high rise in current density, unlike the substrate. This behavior indicates that the coatings partially modify the electrochemical response of the substrate, despite the presence of porosity.

From a functional perspective, this response is particularly significant. Although the coatings exhibit higher  i corr  values than the substrate, their ability to delay the onset of rapid anodic dissolution and to sustain passive-like behavior indicates a fundamentally different corrosion mechanism. Rather than preventing corrosion entirely, the coatings act to control and mitigate corrosion processes, limiting their propagation under aggressive conditions.

Therefore, the results indicate that, while the cold-sprayed coatings do not achieve corrosion resistance comparable to that of hot-rolled AISI 316L, as reported in (Ref  13 ), they exhibit a more noble electrochemical behavior than the SAE 1020 substrate and are able to sustain higher anodic potentials without a significant increase in current density. This suggests that, despite their inherent porosity and microstructural heterogeneity, the coatings can improve certain aspects of the corrosion performance of the substrate, although these features prevent them from reaching the corrosion resistance of the bulk material.

In coatings with higher porosity and interparticle heterogeneity, localized passive film destabilization may occur due to electrolyte penetration through interconnected pores and interparticle boundaries. These regions can act as preferential sites for chloride accumulation and localized electrochemical activity, promoting local breakdown of the protective surface condition under anodic polarization. In addition, pores and heterogeneities associated with the cold spray process may facilitate localized dissolution and hinder the formation of a uniform and stable electrochemical interface. Therefore, the corrosion behavior of the coatings likely results from the competition between localized degradation processes associated with porosity and the tendency of the stainless steel matrix to develop protective surface films.

Therefore, the OCP measurements indicate that the cold-sprayed coatings exhibit a more noble electrochemical behavior than the SAE 1020 substrate, although still less noble than the hot-rolled AISI 316L. The EIS results highlight the strong influence of microstructural heterogeneities inherent to the cold spray process, such as porosity and interparticle boundaries (Ref  3 ,  11 ,  12 ,  25 ,  40 ), leading to lower polarization resistance and higher variability compared to bulk material. In contrast, cyclic polarization tests reveal that the coatings can sustain higher anodic potentials without an abrupt increase in current density compared to the substrate, indicating the development of passive-like behavior.

Taken together, the OCP and EIS results provide a consistent and complementary understanding of the electrochemical behavior of the cold-sprayed coatings. The shift toward more noble OCP values relative to the SAE 1020 substrate indicates that the coatings effectively modify the tendency for corrosion, promoting a more stable electrochemical state. This trend is further supported by the EIS results, which reveal a measurable capacitive response and non-negligible polarization resistance, confirming the ability of the coatings to act as electrochemical barriers. Although the impedance values are lower than those of bulk 316L, the coatings still exhibit sufficient resistance to charge transfer, indicating partial protection of the substrate.

Importantly, the combination of more noble potentials and capacitive behavior suggests that the coatings can develop passive-like surface films, even in the presence of porosity and interparticle boundaries. Therefore, while the microstructural heterogeneity inherent to cold spray influences the magnitude of the electrochemical response, it does not prevent the coatings from fulfilling their primary function. Instead, the results demonstrate that cold-sprayed 316L coatings effectively alter both the thermodynamic and kinetic aspects of corrosion, providing a robust and practical means of enhancing the corrosion resistance of carbon steel substrates.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: 316L coatings were produced by cold spray on SAE 1020 steel, yielding continuous deposits with thicknesses of approximately 450-520  µ m and porosity levels in the range of 5-7 vol.%. The coatings exhibited the characteristic heterogeneous microstructure composed of partially plastically deformed particles, interparticle boundaries, and residual porosity, features inherent of cold spraying process. Increasing the deposition gas temperature promoted a modest reduction in coating porosity, indicating improved particle deformation and interparticle bonding. However, the overall cold-spray microstructural features remained present under all processing conditions. Thus, deposition temperature influenced densification but did not eliminate the intrinsic heterogeneity associated with solid-state particle consolidation. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy revealed that the coatings provide measurable barrier properties, although still markedly inferior to bulk hot-rolled 316L stainless steel. Their lower polarization resistance and higher effective capacitance, relative to wrought 316L, reflect the influence of porosity, interparticle boundaries, and local heterogeneities on electrolyte penetration and charge-transfer processes. Polishing altered the electrochemical interface and shifted OCP to more noble values, but its effect on polarization resistance was not systematic. Cyclic polarization measurements demonstrated that the cold-sprayed coatings can sustain higher anodic potentials than the bare substrate without the abrupt current rise characteristic of active dissolution, indicating passive-like behavior. Although the coatings do not reproduce the corrosion resistance of fully dense bulk 316L, they show strong potential as protective surface layers for chloride-containing environments. Although the coatings do not achieve the corrosion resistance of fully dense bulk AISI 316L, the results indicate that cold-sprayed 316L coatings are promising candidates for improving the corrosion resistance of the coated carbon steel substrates in chloride-containing environments. Future optimization strategies should focus on reducing interconnected porosity and improving interparticle bonding to further enhance the electrochemical performance of the coatings.
